Dots (... indicate missing portions, leaf damage, or unidentified characters;
words or letters enclosed in brackets are my suggestions based on my understanding.
Each folio side generally contains four to seven lines.
In his mouth resides the fortune of speech; in his hands, the fortune of fortune, the fortune of the earth, and the fortune of all-bestowing charity; in his staff, the fortune of heroism;
in the lotus of his heart, the fortune of the forest; at the tip of his sword, the fortune of valor; and upon his entire body, the fortune of all virtues.
[One attains] the gentle splendor (*saumyalakṣmī*), [and] having fully worshipped the victorious splendor (*jaya...sampūjyalakṣmī*). And likewise, [there is] Paṃśaṅka...

In the western quarter (*vāruṇe*) for five months, there shall be Pūrvabhādra. And in the asterism of Revatī (*pauṣṇe*) for one month, and in the quarter of the asterism of Aśvinī (*dyā...pāde*) for three fortnights.
*Paṅkaja*—*Rohiṇī*... [is] a two-footed lunar mansion (*dvipādanakṣatra*). (l. 5) *Vasu*—*Aśvinī* is a two-footed lunar mansion. (l.
6) Having crossed over *Ahirbudhnya*, etc., [there is] a three-footed... (p. 5b, l. 1) [The prayer to Vighneśvara:
A coconut, free from cracks, filled with water, and shaped like a cart (*śakaṭākṛti*).
Exceedingly long, exceedingly sharp, free from impurities, and not immature; well-rounded, rich in even lines, possessing a fine crest, and having beautiful eyes—
one should thus examine the characteristics of a coconut in many ways.
The wise one should strike the moon-peak and offer the nose-less [oblation].
One should strike with the *trayambaka* mantra. If more than three strikes are made, that rite will certainly result in instability.
At the third watch of the night, one should recite that [mantra] one hundred times.
[This results in] the success of the rite being divided into two parts; [otherwise there is] slackness in the rite...
among those [lines], on the line, that [brings about] the destruction of delusion.
If [the mark] is on the right eye, it causes defects.
On the primary line of the eye, there will be danger for the teacher.
With every effort, one should strike the coconut.
And at the mouth of the grain, *turji*... At the mouth, three *svadhā*s.
I shall now proclaim the fire-oblation (*homa*) that bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). (p. 6b, l. 1) (Meditation on the Sacrificial Hall—subheading) Meditation on the Sacrificial Hall.
It has four faces and four gates, a mass of radiance, and is called "matted hair.
There are ivory arches upon its mouths, as well as eyes and mirrors.
Within the body are the arm, the sacrificial pit, the pillar, and the sword; thus it is described.
The leather-bound club, the sacrificial altar, the finger, and likewise the toe; the jar, the flesh-mark, the foot, [the head]...
the cane-work, the gem, the banner, the sky, the garment, the cloth, and the form of the sacrificer’s child.
...the deities.
Meditation on the primordial Great Sadāśiva,
who possesses two thousand arms and is complete with all [attributes].
And [he has] two feet and three eyes; his face is likewise.
[He is adorned] with all ornaments... up to myself.
Thus, to the presiding deities of the sacrifice, to Sadāśiva, obeisance to you!
The gate has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and it is likewise blue and established by Viṣṇu. The stalk [is placed] upon the jars... with stone, brick, and wood.
And all the gods and ṛṣis, together with their sons, [are present] in the *śaktis*.
And one should perform all the ritual procedures of the Tantra with devoted attendants and members of the Gaṇas;
having adorned it with erotic grace (*śṛṅgāra*), one should carry out the rite even without a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
Thus is the form of the gateway. And [one should fashion] the eyes upon the head and the nose... (p. 7b, l. 1).
The meditation of the sacrificial hall,
the deluding meditation, and the meditation of Bṛhaspati.
The meditation on Gaurī, the meditation on Sadāśiva,
and the meditation on the pavilion.
The meditation on Śukra,
the meditation on Naṭeśvara, and the meditation on the Gopura.
The meditation on Uṣā,
the meditation on Aṅgāraka,
and the meditation on Śivakāmasundarī.
The meditation on the stūpa,
the meditation on the dawn,
and the meditation on Saturn.
The meditation on Somāskanda,
the meditation on the celestial chariot...
the meditation.
The meditation on Rāhu, the meditation on Gaurī,
and the meditation on the power of the celestial chariot (vimāna-śakti).
...meditation is the banner-meditation;
that is the meditation on phenomena.
The meditation of the alms-seeker... the meditation on Candraśekhara.
The meditation on Bālasubrahmaṇya (p. 8a, l. 1); the meditation on the five forms.
...meditation on the seat of power,
meditation on Gaṇapati.
The meditation on Gaṇapati... the meditation on the fortress of the village.
The meditation on Subrahmaṇya,
the meditation on the southern face...
the meditation.
The meditation on Mahālakṣmī, the meditation on Devasenā, and the meditation on Viṣṇu.
...the meditation on Śakti,
the meditation on Sarasvatī, and the meditation on Mahāvallī.
Meditation on Brahmā, meditation on the Sun, and meditation on Nandikeśvara.
Meditation on a donkey, meditation on a fortress,
... meditation on a barren woman.
The meditation on Caṇḍeśvara, the meditation on Jaya, and the meditation on the Teacher.
(Vimānapīṭhaśakti) (Side Heading) Meditation on the Power of the Vimānapīṭha:
The pedestal (pīṭha) shall be square; it is here called the stationary liṅga (sthitiliṅga).
A well-rounded seat is prescribed; it may be eighteen-fingered in width. Gaurī is situated upon a circular pedestal (*vṛttapīṭha*), while Bhadrā has a throne-seat (*bhadrapīṭha*) as her seat.
The reclining posture (*śayana*) is on a lotus-pedestal (*padmapīṭha*); this is here called the standing-limb (*sthitilaṅga*).
While reciting the mantra, one should visualize [the goddess] endowed with two arms,
red in color, her body in the triple-bend posture (*tribhaṅga*),
adorned with variegated garments, complete with all ornaments, and beautified by an upward-bound hair-knot.
...abounding in flowers and adorned with soft locks of hair;
[like] a lotus... (p. 9a, l.
1). Having meditated thus specifically upon the *pīṭha-śakti* (l. 2),

...white in appearance, with auspicious eyes, holding a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*) and a blade of *dūrvā* grass in his right [hands], (l. 3) ...holding a skull-cup (*kapāla*) in his left hand, wearing excellent sandals, mounted upon the vehicle of a spirit (*bhūta*), I worship the Lord of the Dancing Mendicant (*Bhikṣāṇṛteśa*). (l. 4)
(Mohinī) (Side heading):
[I meditate on] Mohinī, who is dark-complexioned, whose right hand holds a parrot placed upon her lotus-like face which shines to the right,
whose other foot rests upon the ground behind the first, and whose other limb is slightly bent.
I bow to her who stands at the side of Śambhu, who deludes the world, whose hand resting on his left holds a flower-adorned braid; (l.
4) [I bow to him] who has a single face and three eyes, who is seated comfortably, charming, and holding a beautiful book... (l. 5).
One should meditate on her who has the form of a pavilion adorned with all ornaments,
radiant with a crown, holding a blue lotus in her left hand,
and [the goddess] Lambā on the right side for the protection of the world.

At dawn, having meditated upon the purifier of the world, who possesses three high triplets of limbs, whose hands are like lotuses, who holds a mirror in her right hand, and whose rays are beloved by the Sun— (l. 4–5).

I worship Śiva-Sūrya, who has two eyes and two hands, possesses a *puṣpaka* [flower], wears earrings, stands with feet even, is red in color, and is captivating; he is mounted upon a circular chariot on the head.
Meditation on the Sun:
Two-armed, with a lotus in hand, having a red-colored form, seated upon a chariot drawn by seven horses—meditate on Bhāskara, the remover of sins. (1.2)

Having placed [the deity] in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) or, alternatively, upon a lion throne (*siṃhāsana*), one should perform the entire commencement according to the previously mentioned procedure. Homage to the Sun.
Meditation on the Moon.
...to Soma, who has two eyes and is white in color; (l.
5) who wears white garments... [the] god, likewise with a white-colored chariot;
having a white parasol and banner, and ten white horses... (l. 6)
One should see the rope, the two-armed [deity], and likewise the kumuda;
[the mandala] is four-cornered...
facing westward, and proceeding clockwise around the mountains.
The lineage is Āgneya... extending over ten kingdoms. The *gotra* is Ātreya, and the birth sign is Kṛttikā.
Thus it is recited. Having meditated upon Soma, I bow to him: *Oṃ saṃ somāya namaḥ*.
Meditative concentration.
Likewise, one should visualize Budha as having one face and two eyes, yellow in color,
wearing yellow garments, and beautifully adorned with a yellow umbrella.
Wearing yellow garments and likewise holding a bow and arrow,
he is seated upon a heroic lion-throne in the center of the arrow-shaped [mandala].

Facing eastward in this manner, situated in the direction of Īśāna, [he is] the lord of Magadha and likewise the one who circumambulates the mountains; belonging to the lineage of Ātreya and having Śravaṇa as his birth star—
such is the meditation on Budha.
Homage... Oṃ buṃ, homage to Budha. (l.4) The meditation on Bṛhaspati.
...of yellow color, with one face and four arms;
wearing yellow garments and being yellow in hue...
[he holds] a yellow parasol and banner, situated in the center of the four-peaked [mandala].
...likewise equal to the seat of enjoyments.
[He holds] the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), as well as a rosary (*akṣasūtra*) and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
In the northern region... clockwise. And in the lands of Sindhu, sovereignty.
The lineage of Aṅgiras, the daughter of Dakṣa, and likewise the preceptor of the gods—having thus bowed to Bṛhaspati in this manner, [I say]: "Salutation to Bṛhaspati.
This is the meditation on Śukra.
White in color, with Śukra, having one face and two hands,
endowed with a white garment, joined with a single-faced [deity]...
and possessing a white parasol and banner, he is the sovereign wearing white garments.
In the center of the five-cornered [mandala], he is seated upon a variegated lion-throne,
facing eastward, with his hands holding a mace and a lotus;
likewise, one should circumambulate the Lord of the Gaṇas and the mountains.

The birth-chart of Jupiter is associated with the *gotrabhārgava* [constellation] and the *jyeṣṭhā* asterism; he is the ninth [planet] situated in the eastern direction, and likewise the preceptor of the *rākṣasas*. Having described him in such a manner, I bow to the Blessed Śukra. Oṃ, obeisance to Śukra.
The meditation on Guru Aṅgāraka:
...two-eyed, with one face and four arms;
wearing red garments and likewise red... [complexion].
[He who has] a red parasol and banner, and who holds a spear, trident, and mace;
[who is] triangular in shape and facing [the practitioner];
and who performs the circumambulation of the mountain, situated in the southern direction.
...and likewise the lineage of Bhāradvāja;
and having Aśvinī as his birth [constellation], I bow to Aṅgāraka.
Homage to Aṅgāraka! (l. 2–3)
The meditation on Śanaiścara:
He has one face, two eyes, and two arms; he is black in complexion, wears black garments, and likewise possesses a black banner.
And [he sees] a black-colored chariot, with a mandala in the shape of a bow;
seated upon a black lion-throne in the center, facing westward,
and holding a trident and a bow, he is stationed in the western direction.
I bow to him who is the lord of Ādhra-deśa, who circumambulates the mountains,
who belongs to the Kāśyapa lineage, whose birth sign is Revatī,
and whose vehicle is the vulture— having thus meditated upon Śani, I pay homage.
Oṃ śaṃ, homage to Śanaiścara. (l. 3) The meditation on Rāhu: two-eyed, blue-colored, three-armed, and one-faced.
Wearing blue garments and [having] blue...
[the lord of the quarters], with a blue parasol and banner, and the mandala of the black winnowing basket;
likewise, [he is seated] upon a blue lion-throne, facing south.
And likewise the lord of the eastern region, Śūlaka;
and having circumambulated Girī, [I bow to] Ajayamani of the Gotra...
Or, having meditated upon Rāhu, I pay homage.
Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to Rāhu.
... (Ketu) meditation:
[He is] of variegated color, two-armed, and one-faced.
[He should offer] variegated garments... and likewise a variegated umbrella and banner;
in the mandala, a banner-shaped [object], as well as a sacred seat (*pavitrāsana*).
And likewise the lord of the forest region, situated in the northwestern direction.
The birth [of Ketu] occurs under the asterism Āśleṣā, on a variegated lion-throne.
Having meditated upon these two syllables— the Lord who has performed the circumambulation of the mountains twice— I pay homage to Ketu.
Oṃ, obeisance to Ketu. (l. 2) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Candraśekhara.
[He who possesses] a broad face and eyes, and a gentle, amorous grace.
[He who has] the gesture of granting boons (*varada-hasta*) and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), whose crown is adorned with the moon... (l.
3), whose body is straight, whose feet are even, standing in the *sthānaka* posture, having the luster of coral, (l.
4) bearing an axe..., and seated upon a lotus pedestal.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Candraśekhara. ...obeisance to the seat of Gaurī.
[She is] dark-complexioned, two-eyed, two-armed, and with two bends of the body... [holding] a lotus in her right hand, adorned with bracelets on her left wrist.
(Side heading) (Naṭeśvara) Praise... Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Gaurī. (l. 2) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Naṭeśvara.
...The matted hair, the moon, the goldsmith, the skull, the bone, the gods, and the river. (l. 3)
[He is] like a white *arka* tree, with a crown of tawny hair, wearing three garments;
holding a *ḍamaru* drum in both his right and left hands, and extending his left [hand]...
(l. 4) ...holding fire in his left, reclining upon a green [surface], situated on the back of a goat covered in ash. (l. 5)
Having bent his own foot and raised it so that its radiance rests between the left [thighs],
he wears a sandal whose tip flashes with the sound of "maṇi maṇi" from the jewels of his banner-bells.
On the right ear is a crocodile-shaped earring, while on the left earlobe is one adorned with a leaf-pattern.
I salute Naṭeśa Śiva, smeared with ashes, possessing ten million forms, and having three eyes.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Naṭeśvara. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śivakāmasundarī.
Standing indeed on the left side of Śambhu is Gaurī, who has two eyes and two arms, joined with [her consort]... (l.
3) ...both having hair tied up and adorned with crowns.

And Kuśasundarī [is placed] at his right... his foot [is] raised from thirst (*udanya*). It should be joined as either bent or hanging down... [she is] bearing a flower, provided with bracelets. (l. 5) Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śivakāmasundarī. (p. 16a, l. 1) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Somāskanda.

Kṛṣṇa, whose left foot is supported by Dakṣa and who is asleep, and who holds a deer, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), an axe (*ṭaṅka*), and a boon (*vara*) in his [right hands], together with the Goddess, whose other two feet are supported by his left arm and are asleep, [is situated] in the center. (ll. 2–3)
I worship Guheśa together with Umā and Skanda.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Somāskanda. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Gaurī’s seat.
[She is] two-armed, with a beautiful face, and endowed with two eyes. (l. 5)
The goddess is adorned with a crown and a basket-shaped ornament (*karaṇḍa*), her dark blue locks reaching down to her waist;
she possesses a broad forehead marked by the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft and is endowed with the first [of the auspicious] marks such as the *prāsāda*.
With her right hand lowered, the goddess is decorated with all ornaments. (Side heading: Taniyadharman, Bālasubrahmaṇya)
Having meditated upon the goddess whose face is like fine silk, one should worship her with perfumes and other offerings:
*oṃ hrīṃ gaurīyai namaḥ*.
She is exceedingly slender, dark-complexioned, two-eyed, two-armed, and possesses two bends of the body.
With her right and left feet standing with the [right] one slightly bent,
and with her two hands— [the right] holding a blue lotus and the other extended downward— the Supreme Goddess should be [visualized].
[She is accompanied by] the youthful Subrahmaṇya.
...the two-eyed, beautiful Subrahmaṇya, with two lotuses in his hands... that is the deity Skanda.
Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Subrahmaṇya. (l. 5–6)
I bow to him who has one face and two eyes, who brings joy to the brahmins, and whose radiance is equal to that of a child.
(Pañcamūrttigaṇapati) Oṃ Gaṃ... salutation to the form of Gaṇapati.
Gajānana has one tusk, while Samadanta has three eyes. (l.
2) ...He is of elemental form, possesses a large belly, wears a snake as a sacred thread, and is like a mass of clouds.
(l. 3) They are seated in the lotus posture; their left feet are extended here and there, while the right [feet] are [bent]. (l. 4)
One should fashion his own tooth as a ring on the left hand and an axe in the right;
one should provide a rosary and a sweetmeat (*laḍḍuka*) in the two left hands and in the two right hands.
In the great *liṅga*, there is a casket (*karaṇḍaka*), adorned with necklaces and other ornaments.
Thus has Gaṇapati been described. When [he is] situated upon a lotus-seat, he dances with four arms at his sides and everywhere has the mouse as his vehicle.
Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Oṃ sāṃ, obeisance to Śakunī. Starting from the east: Oṃ gāṃ, [obeisance to] Hastin.
Oṃ gāṃ, obeisance to Lambodara... the Vināyakas. Oṃ gāṃ, Pañcā... (l. 5).
Oṃ gāṃ, obeisance to Vighneśvara. Ekadanta... (l. 6). Oṃ gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati... having worshipped the offerings of food.
(p. 18a, l. 1) (Side heading) (Dakṣiṇāmūrti)
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

He should have four arms and three eyes, with matted locks hanging down. With two hands, he holds [implements] on the right side of fire; [one hand] is endowed with a ring. In the left hand there is a book, and on the other side, the right hand holds a staff (*gada*), while the left hand holds a trident (*triśūla*).
With his right leg hanging down and his left foot adorned,
wearing a garment of tiger skin and decorated with all ornaments,
he is situated at the foot of a banyan tree on that Mount Kailāsa.
Jamadagni is on the right of Sṛṣṭi in the Tanu and other [mantras];
Bhāradvāja is on the right of Agasti, and also on the right of Bhārgava.
Such is the form of the exposition, which has Dakṣiṇāmūrti as its presiding deity.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the Goddess. Starting from the east: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ananta... Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the form of Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu has four arms; he wears a crown and holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, seated upon the throne of Garuḍa:
*Oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. (l. 3) In the east—*śrīmahālakṣmyai namaḥ*. Starting from the east: *keśavāya*, *garuḍadhvajāya*. (l. 4)

In the north: *śrīkamalāyai namaḥ*. *oṃ hāṃ kṛṣṇāya namaḥ*. To Mādhava. To Acyuta, *namaḥ*. (l. 5) To Vaikuṇṭha. To Govinda. To Dāmodara. [These] are to be worshipped. (p. 19b, l. 1) (Side heading) (Brahmā)()

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Brahmā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Brahmā. [He is] four-faced and four-armed, adorned with a crown of matted hair, possessing eight eyes, golden-hued, and wearing a divine sacred thread.
Carrying an *abhaya* [mudrā] and a rosary in his right hands,
holding a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in the left, with the lotus of his hand resting on his hip;
he is accompanied by Gāyatrī, Sarasvatī, and Sāvitrī.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā. (l. 5) To the east: śrīṃ... salutation. To the north: śrīṃ, salutation to Gāyatrī. To the south: śrīṃ, salutation to Sāvitrī. (p. 20a, l. 1) From the east onwards... salutation to Sanātana. (l. 2) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Jyeṣṭha. ...ne salutation. (l. 3) Salutation to Bhūsura. Salutation to Dhātṛ. (l. 4) Salutation to Caturmukha. Having thus performed the worship.
॥ Svayambhuva ॥ Dhātābjāya (p. 20b, l. 1) (Side heading) (Durgā):
Oṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Durgā. Oṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the form of Durgā.
[She who is] seated comfortably, with hair like blue lotus petals, and having the appearance of a blue lotus petal. (l. 2)
She has a beautiful face, is adorned with all ornaments,
and possesses four arms holding a discus, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a conch, and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*).
She is bound at the waist by her breasts and stands upon the head of Mahiṣa.

Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Durgā. Having worshipped [her], [one should worship]: Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the Power of the Seat (pīṭhaśakti). Starting from the east: Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Ṛddhi and Buddhi... salutation to the Goddess. Salutation to Vallisenānī. Salutation to Lakṣmīśakti. Having thus worshipped, [one should worship] salutation to Puṣkalaśakti. Salutation to Vaṭukaśakti.
Salutation to Vīraśakti. (p.21a, l.1) (Side heading) [Durgā] ...four-armed and endowed with a crown.
One should meditate upon the Goddess who holds a conch and a discus, who grants fearlessness, and whose hand rests upon her hip;
[and] even though [she stands] upon a buffalo, [the latter] has its head [bowed] above [her].
Having thus visualized Durgā, who bestows the fruits of righteous action upon herself, one should remember her.
Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Durgā.
She holds a lotus and a rosary in her upper hands,
possesses dark limbs and beautiful eyes, and is enriched by the three [eyes].
I praise Karaṇḍikā, who possesses the splendor of a fierce crescent moon, the glorious treasury of desire, the union of Śiva and Śakti.
(Side heading: The Teacher, Abundant in Hari and Hara) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Seat of the Teacher. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Form of the Teacher.

With a body of dark complexion and in the full bloom of youth, holding a lofty lotus in his hand; with his lotus-feet encircled by a garland of sesame seeds, he sits in the blissful posture (*sukhāsana*),
with his left and right [hands] abundant and full.
In the north: Oṃ śraṃ, obeisance to the seat of Puṣkala; Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to the form of Puṣkali.
[One should visualize] the goddess Sumukhī, dark-complexioned, wearing golden garments, two-eyed, two-armed, gentle, and adorned with all ornaments.
Her limbs are anointed with divine perfumes and adorned [with ornaments].
A flower is held in her right hand, while in her left is a...
[ornament]. Her left leg is extended, while the right is bent.
Or likewise, [one] with conch-like ears and earrings;
having meditated thus in particular, one should worship Puṣkalā in the north.
Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Puṣkalā.
On the right: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Pūrṇāsana. Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Pūrṇāmūrti.
Pūrṇā has a golden luster and wears garments of dark blue;
in her left hand she holds a flower, and in her right she holds a bracelet.
The left foot should be drawn up and the right one should hang down;
this is called the lion-ear (*siṃhakuṇḍala*) as well as the crocodile-ear (*makarakuṇḍala*).
Having meditated thus with particular care, one should worship the Mistress of the Complete Scripture (*pūrṇaśāstreśvarī*).
Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Pūrṇā. Having worshipped [her], [one worships] starting from the east: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mannātha (or Anātha); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaha; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapālaka; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vīrabhadra," [one should worship]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the one whose seat is the bull (vṛṣabhāsana). "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the bull (vṛṣabhamūrti). [He who is] four-footed, the embodiment of the Vedas, the form of fire, whose stability is fire, whose eyes are Agni, and whose face is Rudra; [he who is] the form of Brahmā and Viṣṇu... "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the bull (vṛṣabha)."
Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the one whose seat is the bull and power (*vṛṣabha-śakty-āsana*). Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the form of the bull and power (*vṛṣabha-śakti-mūrti*).

With flaming hair rising upward, beautiful fangs, and a nose curved like a Veda, holding an arrow, a bow, and the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness—[these are] on the bull and power to the left of the Bull-God (*vṛṣadeva*).

Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Vṛṣabhaśakti. Having worshipped [her], [one should worship] in the east: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Uṣā and Gopati. [One should worship] Bhṛṅgin, Nandin, Vṛṣāpati, Vṛṣāṇin, and Śaṅkhukarṇa—[the latter] possessing the luster of collyrium, with three eyes like fire, and bearing camphor and sandalwood.
I salute the splendor of Kastūrikā, Kuṅkumapañca, Vṛṣabhaśakti, and Añjanādevī.
(Sūrya) Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Sun (arkāsana). Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to the form of the Sun (arkamūrti).
Two-armed, with a lotus in his hand, having a red-colored form,
endowed with a crown-jar (*karaṇḍa-makuṭa*), adorned with all ornaments,
and situated in the midst of a circle of light whose radiance is twice that of his crown.
The goddesses Uṣā and Pratyūṣā are stationed on the left and right;
having placed Aruṇa, whose form is deep red, in front,
[one should meditate upon] the Sun, the remover of sins, seated in his chariot drawn by seven horses.
Having placed [the deity] in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) or on the lion throne (*siṃhāsana*),
one should worship all the Ādityas according to the previously mentioned procedure:
*Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Arka*.

In the south, *namaḥ* to Uṣādevī; in the north, *namaḥ* to Pratyuṣādevī. From the east onwards: *oṃ saṃ* to Soma, *namaḥ*; *oṃ aṃ* to Aṅgāraka, *namaḥ*; *oṃ buṃ* to Budha, *namaḥ*; *bṛṃ* to Bṛhaspati, *namaḥ*; *bhaṃ* to Bhārgava, *namaḥ*; *śaṃ* to Śanīśvara, *namaḥ*; *raṃ* to Rāhu, *namaḥ*; *kaṃ* to Ketu, *namaḥ*.
Having thus worshipped: *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the seat of Bhairava; *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the form of Bhairava.

[I worship him] who bears matted locks of red flames, who wears the moon, whose body is composed of red radiance, who holds in his hands a trident, a skull-cup, a noose, and a *ḍamaru* drum, and who effects the protection of the world.
I bow to Nirvāṇa, the one with the dog as his vehicle, the three-eyed one, the tumultuous joy;
I bow to the auspicious Vaṭuka, the protector of the field, who is honored by spirits and piśācas.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhairava!
Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Raktashakti. (L. 2) Starting from the east: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Asitāṅgabhairava; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rurubhairava; (L.
3) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍabhairava; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Krodhabhairava; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Unmattabhairava. (L. 4)
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kapālabhairava. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhīṣaṇabhairava. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Saṃhārabhairava. Having thus performed the worship. (Side heading:
Balipīṭha)
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the auspicious form of the Liṅga... Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the auspicious embodiment of the Liṅga.
With feet bound in the lotus-posture (*padmabandha*), [he holds] abundant nectar;
beautiful with anklets, a *kumuda*-flower, and ear-flaps.
My [liṅga] has the form of a metre, possesses eight corners, and indeed consists of eight petals;
it has the form of an auspicious liṅga situated above the auspicious pericarp of the bond;
it has five heads, four faces, and eyes together with the nose.
Ten-armed, ten-piercing, ten-eared, and ten-bearing;
with a single throat and a heart of exceedingly red color;
with two feet—such is the form of the sacrificial pedestal for the offering to the spirits (*bhūtabali*).
Homage to the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*). Having worshipped it,
[one should worship] Bali, who possesses flaming goads and deer-like tusks,
adorned with various ornaments, and joined with hands holding the Vedas.
[The worshipper should visualize] the ascetic-moon bearing arrows and a bow, the pedestal-power (*pīṭhaśakti*) of the Bhūtas and others, and the sacrificial offering (*bali*).
(Side heading: Durgā) Oṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Durgā. Oṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the form of Durgā.
[He is] one with upward-pointing hair, beautiful fangs, and endowed with a fierce gaze.
With the right foot extended and the left foot reclining,
he holds a trident and a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*) in his right hands, and a noose and a skull-cup (*kapāla*) in his left.
A *vetāla* is at his left ear, while a *preta* serves as an earring on his right.
Possessing a great form of blue color, adorned with a garland of skulls, and endowed with all ornaments—may they protect the village at all times.
Oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Durgā. (Side heading)

(Mahālakṣmī): Oṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Mahālakṣmī. Oṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the form of Mahālakṣmī. [One should meditate upon] the four-armed Mahālakṣmī, who likewise bestows the gestures of fearlessness and boons. (l. 2)

I meditate upon the beloved of Govinda, who sits in the lotus posture, holds a lotus in her hand, is as radiant as water, and has large eyes like the calyx of a lotus. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī.
Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Sarasvatī. Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the form of Sarasvatī.
[One should meditate on] Sarasvatī with four arms, adorned with a crown of matted hair, holding a water-pot and a rosary in her two right and left hands respectively.
She has a book in her right hand and [a rosary] in her left hand;
she is adorned with crocodile earrings, necklaces, and armlets;
she is endowed with the nine heroic sentiments (*navavīra*), possesses one face and two eyes.
White in color and of magnificent form, with a yellow garment as an upper robe;
seated upon a lotus throne with two feet, the right foot raised three times higher;
endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
"Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī. Having thus worshipped her:
"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Nandikeśvara. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Nandikeśvara, who bears an axe and a deer in his palms, and performs the añjali gesture of salutation to Īśa."
I worship the illustrious Nandikeśa, whose forehead is white with the smearing of ashes like a crescent moon, who is radiant with the matted locks of the Gaṅgā,
who is the destroyer of Tripura in his various manifestations, the preeminent leader of the Pramathas, the lord of the Gaṇas,
and whose lotus feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nandikeśvara. Having worshipped [him], [one worships] obeisance to Nandiśakti. Having worshipped [her], Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Caṇḍeśvara.
In the Kali age, [the deity] is two-armed, peaceful, and adorned with all ornaments. (l.
3) If [the posture is] *bhaṅga*, the right foot is [extended] together with the left foot and hand; (l.
4) or the right foot is standing, while the [left] well-placed lotus is bent.
Vīracaṇḍeśa is naked, or else he is covered by breasts. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Caṇḍeśvara.
He has two eyes, two arms, is dark-complexioned, and indeed holds a ṭaṅka-axe.

Having two feet, hands joined in the añjali gesture, adorned with all ornaments, and endowed with a crown of matted hair—this is remembered as the fierce form (Caṇḍarūpa). (p. 27b, l. 1) (Side heading:
Gaṇapati-Vighnaśakti)
Oṃ gaṃ, homage to the seat of Gaṇapati. Oṃ gaṃ, homage to the form of Gaṇapati.
He whose eyes are the sun, the lotus, and fire; who possesses a crest-jewel shining like ten million [suns] and a hand;
who is beautiful with the face of the lord of serpents; and who holds in his two hands the goad, the lotus, and the noose.

I worship him who holds a tusk and a beautiful sweetmeat in his two hands, whose waist is adorned with a girdle and a garland, and whose arms are joined by a sacred thread. Oṃ Gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati. Oṃ Sāṃ, salutation to the Śakti-seat.

I worship the goddess Buddhi, who is present on the left side of the god, holding a blue lotus in her right hand, with her left arm extended, resembling gold in complexion. [She is] present on the left side of the god, holding a blue lotus in her right hand.
I worship Buddhi, who resembles gold and has her left hand extended; (p.28a, l.1) (Side heading) (The Meditation on Guhā):
*Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Śakti. Having performed the worship:
In the east: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Elephant-faced One; to the Long-lipped One; to Vighneśvara; to Gaṇādhipati; to Vināyaka, obeisance; to the Single-tusked One; to the Lover of Edibles;
to the Five-handed One—having worshipped [these].

Oṃ sāṃ, salutation to the one whose seat is the cave. Oṃ sāṃ, salutation to the form of Guha. (L. 4) Holding a rosary in his right hand and a small bell in the other hand, with one hand placed upon his left thigh and the other joined with the gesture of protection (*abhaya*), he has the luster of coral.

I praise the Youthful One (*Kumāra*), who has a beautiful face, lotus-like eyes, and wears a crown shaped like a casket; who is accompanied on both sides by the goddess Senā and the creeper-like Vallī, and whose waist is adorned with a shining girdle. Oṃ sāṃ, homage to Guha. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Devasenā.
Yellow in complexion, holding a blue lotus, the daughter of Śacī, adorned with divine garments;
with a long garland hanging from her left [hand], the daughter of Mahendra, wearing a wreath of Mandāra flowers;
her sandals worshipped by the gods, moon-faced, she stands at the side of Senānī Vāyu.
Worship the goddess who is adorned with a pearl necklace, who has two eyes, and who is in the *tribhaṅgī* posture.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Devasenā. To the right—Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the seat of Mahābalī. Oṃ hrīṃ...
Dark-complexioned, holding a lotus, her ears radiant with jeweled earrings,
with a long garland hanging from her right hand, wearing a basket-shaped crown, and her breasts adorned with fine keys;
she stands on the left side of the one born in the Śara forest, gazing intently at him.
One should meditate upon Vallīśvarī, who has a garland illuminated by lightning and a moon-like face.
(l. 3) Oṃ hrīṃ mahābalāyai namaḥ. To the east and so forth: Oṃ jayantāya namaḥ; aṃ agniśikhāya namaḥ; (l. 4) kaṃ kṛttikāputrāya namaḥ.
*Bhaṃ* to the Lord of Beings, obeisance! *Saṃ* to the Commander of the Army, obeisance! *Gaṃ* to the Secret One, obeisance! *Haṃ* to the Golden Trident-bearer, obeisance!
*Vaṃ* to the Wide-eyed One, obeisance! Having thus worshipped:
*Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the Staff-seated One; *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the Form of the Staff-bearer.
Four-armed, three-eyed, and dark-complexioned, wearing matted locks,
adorned with all ornaments, possessing a fierce form;
holding a staff and a skull in his left hands, and a needle in his right hand.
A trident in the right hand and a *ḍamaru* drum in the left hand;
the right and left feet are raised, with the soles of the feet resting upon the left [hand].
At the tips of the mace are bud-like shapes, and at the tips of the feet is the coiling of a serpent.
With his left foot drawn up and hanging from a garland of skulls,
with a long lower garment as an upper cloth, and adorned with all ornaments;
on his right side is Daṇḍin, and on his left side is Muṇḍin.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍin. In the space between those [two]: Oṃ jaṃ, obeisance to Jayāsana; Oṃ jaṃ, obeisance to Jayamūrti.
He has three eyes and bears a conch, a discus, and matted locks.
With a face terrifying with fangs, having a fearsome and fierce form,
holding a goad in his right hand and a noose in his left hand;
Jayā on the right side and Vijayā on the left side.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Jayā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of Muṇḍin. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Muṇḍin. (l.
5) Four-armed, three-eyed, red in color, and wearing matted locks;
fully adorned with all ornaments, yet terrifying and of a fierce appearance. (l. 6)
She has a shaven head and holds a staff in her left hand, or else she holds a needle;
in her right hand she holds a goad, accompanied by a noose in her left hand.
Her left foot is raised, while the tips of her feet rest upon a staff.
At the tips of his maces he has the form of buds; at the tips of his feet, he is encircled by mustard seeds.
His right foot is bent, and he is draped with a garland of skulls. He wears a long lower garment as an upper cloth and is adorned with all ornaments.
Muṇḍin on the left side and Daṇḍin on the right side.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Muṇḍin. Oṃ viṃ, obeisance to the Vijayāsana. Oṃ viṃ, obeisance to the form of Vijayā.
Four-armed and three-eyed, dark-complexioned, and wearing matted locks; with a face formidable with fangs, terrifying and of a fierce form;
holding a noose in the right hand and a goad in the left hand.
Vijayā on the left side and Jayā on the right side. (l.
2) Having worshipped with "Oṃ Viṃ, obeisance to Vijayā," (l.
3) [follows] the meditation on the Lord of the Assembly (Sabhāpati).

The handrum is the form of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), while the fire-form is withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). The serpent-mouthed [hand] is the form of persistence (*sthiti*), and the clenched [fist] is concealment (*tirobhāva*). The gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and that of grace (*anugraha*)—these constitute the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*).
The creation of the bond of curiosity within the interval of the bath;
the non-heavy dissolution (*saṃhāra*) consisting of the application of camphor;
and finally, the grace (*anugraha*) which is the witnessing of the dance at dawn. *(Side heading)*
(Mūṣika, Kailāsanandin: The meditation on the mouse:
the tongue, the teeth, the southern [direction], and likewise the mouth and the southwestern [direction].
The eyes are day and night; the two ears are the deity Vāyu.
The body is the cosmic egg (bhuvanāṇḍa), and the hair is known as the Munis along with the Vidyādharas. The tail is Ananta, and the four feet are the four Vedas.
"Brahmā and Viṣṇu are [manifestations] of the individual soul (*jīva*), as is the rat itself.
Homage to the Rat.
Meditation on Nandikeśvara.
The sun is the flame on the lotus of the Vedas, the moon is the path of his eyes;
Rudra is his head and face, and the Aśvinīs are the form of his ears.
He wears anklets of nine-jeweled golden garlands and divine gems.
I bow to Dakṣarāja, whose body is as white as crystal. (l. 2) Regarding the meditation on Siṃha:
the face shall be Vīrabhadra, and the eye shall indeed be Fire itself.
One should place Danta and Aṣṭaśaila on the tongue, and Kāla likewise;
Roma and Deharṣi, and Yama as the four-footed [deity].
One should likewise place Jihva, Prāṇa, Lakṣmī, and Sva on the tail.
Thus has been declared the Lion [Mudrā] by the wise and supreme teacher. Homage to Siṃha! (p. 32b, l. 1) (Side heading) (Mayūra):
The meditation on Mayūra—
In the crest-lock is the partless [Brahman], and the head is indeed the cosmic egg;
the teeth, nose, and tongue are Brahmā and Viṣṇu; and the two eyes are Indra.
(1.2) The two eyes are the sun and the moon, and wind and fire are in the two ears. (1.3)
The two wings are the world of the Vedas and the Śāstras;
the two limbs are devotion and the sages; the two feet are the lunar mansions and the body hair; O Great-Souled One, [he is] dark-complexioned and possesses the meditation upon the peacock.
Oṃ sāṃ, homage to the Peacock. (Side heading:
Vighneśvara, the Six-faced One) The elephant-faced one with three eyes, the color of saffron, possessing four arms.

In his right [hands] he holds a tooth and a noose; in his left, a goad and a sweetmeat (*laḍḍuka*). His hands display the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons. He is praised as possessing a vajra and a spear.
He has an even body, stands with feet together, has the luster of coral, and possesses three eyes.
I bow to the Lord of the entire world in the form of Skanda, who is beautiful in all his youth, adorned with earrings and a basket,
possessing six faces, mounted upon a peacock, having three eyes, and decorated with yellow garments.

One should meditate upon Skanda, the son of Śiva, who is superior even to the gods, the bestower of desired accomplishments, and the consort of Umā-Maheśvara; he always holds a conch, a discus, a sword, and a spear, as well as the gesture of granting boons, in his arms.
[Side heading] (Umāmaheśvara, Śokkapāṇi) [Side heading] Meditation on Umāmaheśvara.
The Lord has one face, four arms, and resembles coral; he holds a black antelope, an axe, a skull-bowl, and displays the gesture of fearlessness. His left leg is extended and rests upon a serpent.
Wearing a crown joined with the moon and accompanied by the daughter of Śakti;
*Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Umāmaheśvara*. This is the visualization for Śokkapāṇi.
One-footed, with eighteen arms and eighteen tridents, with five heads and fifteen eyes,
with wide-open mouths, possessing the fire of the sacrificial hearth and the moon as his eye—
(the King of Weapons).
With hair blazing upward, he bears the emblem of the fire of awakened intellect.
One should fashion a palm-tree staff from that very wood of the *bimba* tree, measuring exactly one cubit (*hasta*).
One should bind it with a cord and attach a palm-leaf fan to the leather.
The meditation on the King of Weapons (Astrarāja):

the path of principles (tattvādhvan), the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), the path of mantras (mantrādhvan), and the path of kalās (kalādhvan).
Homage to the one who sits upon the trident weapon (triśūlāstrāsana).
Having a radiance equal to the midday sun, bearing the moon, intensified by a terrifying laugh,
three-eyed, adorned with *punnāga* flowers, holding a deer, blazing with tawny [hair],
with hair on his head, holding a trident, a mace, a great bell, and a skull-cup with his lotus-like hands.

Having seen that which causes extremely fierce fear, I worship the form of the divine weapon of Paśupati. (Side heading: [The Banner Staff, Vighneśvara]) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the one seated on the trident. The meditation on the banner staff:
One-footed, two-armed, and two-eyed;
adorned with a line of hair like a blade of *darbha* grass;
white-bodied and possessing a parrot-like nose.
Having worshipped Sadāśiva in the form of a staff upon which a lotus seat is mounted,
[one should perform] the meditation on Vighneśvara:
He has one face, three eyes, and an elephantine countenance; he is red in color and possesses four hands.
In his left hand he holds a sweetmeat ball (*laḍḍuka*), and in his other [right] hands he bears a tusk and a goad.
With his left leg bent and resting upon the other foot, he stands with one foot raised and placed firmly upon the ground.
One should constantly meditate upon Vighneśvara, who has a short trunk and ears like winnowing baskets.
(Mayil Yānai, Brahmā)
Mayūradhyāna: Having bowed down to the peacock—seated upon a variegated lion-throne, holding a snake in its beak, possessed of great strength and a massive body—I [offer praise]. (l. 2)
The Meditation on Gajendra: Born of the lineage of Airāvata, white in form, and possessed of great strength;
endowed with four tusks and adorned with all ornaments.
Brahmā—
four-faced, four-armed, endowed with four crowns,
with two eyes in each face, and adorned with muñja grass and darbha blades.
In the right [hand] is a rosary, and in the left hand a *gaṇḍikā*.
In the right [hand] is the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the left hand holds a club (*ūra*). (Side heading:
The Gatekeeper Muṇḍin and Daṇḍin)
The form of Brahmā is traditionally remembered as being endowed with all ornaments;
[the form of] Muṇḍin is black in color, two-armed, and two-eyed.
Equipped with a staff as a weapon, adorned with serpent ornaments,
astonished, and joined by a hand— such is the form of the shaven-headed ones;
this is the meditation on Daṇḍin.
Red in color, with two eyes, and having a serpent as his sacred thread;
possessing a terrifying form with fierce fangs, he has one face and four arms.
He is filled with wonder, his hands joined together, and equipped with a staff as a weapon.
The deity standing on the left side has the form of a staff-bearer (*daṇḍin*). (Subheading:
*Muṇḍi* and *Daṇḍi*) Furthermore, the meditation on *Muṇḍi*:
Extremely fierce, black in color, with four arms and two eyes,
equipped with a staff as a weapon, adorned with serpent ornaments,
wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, filled with wonder, and smeared with ashes.
The deity situated on the left side has the form of a shaven-headed ascetic; he is two-armed, carries a staff,
is red in color, possesses two eyes, and wears a snake as his sacred thread.
[He is] of terrifying form, with excellent fangs, two arms, and one face;
[he is] amazed, joined by hands, and endowed with a staff weapon. The female gatekeeper stands on his left, possessing her own natural form and holding a staff. (Side heading)
(Naṭeśa, Vighneśvara, Gaṇanātha, Bālagaṇapati).
The meditation on Naṭeśa:
One-faced, four-armed, and three-eyed, with a water-jar (*durdhūraka*) in his left hand.

I bow to Naṭeśa, whose hair is matted, who stands with his body smeared with ashes, whose hands are outstretched like moonbeams, whose right foot is raised and bent, who wears an auspicious earring on his left ear, and who bears a hand-drum upon his head that supports the Gaṅgā.
The elephant-faced one, served by hosts of spirits, who feeds on the essence of the kapittha and jambu fruits, the son of Umā, the cause of the destruction of sorrow. (l. 5)
I bow to the lotus feet of Vighneśvara,
which are saffron-colored, endowed with four arms,
and adorned with a crown featuring elephant faces and a casket.
Holding a goad, a sweetmeat, a tusk, and a noose;
possessing a form like fire, the very nature of Gaṇanātha;
with a plantain, a mango, a lotus, a sugarcane, and a modaka in his hand. (l. 7)
I bow to the god Bālasūryaprabha, the youthful Lord of the Gaṇas,
who is endowed with a red complexion and seated upon a beautiful throne.
He has four arms and three eyes, wears a serpent as a sacred thread,
has a protruding lip, and an elephant-like trunk; he holds parched grain and a wood-apple fruit,
while on his left side, in his two hands, he holds a sweetmeat ball (*laḍḍuka*) and a *ketakī* flower.
Likewise, on the right side, one should likewise place Amṛtā holding a tooth-brush;
she is adorned with a basket and a crown and measures five tālas in height.
One should also perform the placement of Gaṇeśa together with her on the right.
[He saw] the Bodhamantra and the mudrā, the lotus that performs all [deeds] like fire;
the Sage situated near a banyan tree—therefore, from him, the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrtti, who is adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads... [he received the teaching].
Viṣṇu— the god wearing yellow garments, adorned with a crown of jewels and gold,
bearing the conch and discus, possessing a dark complexion, and having three eyes— is the supreme boon.
[He saw] Viṣṇu, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, accompanied by Lakṣmī and the goddess Bhūdevī; [and] Brahmā,
wearing a white sacred thread and holding a water-pot and a rosary.
With feet together, yellow-colored... (l. 2) the ninefold Sāvitrī-śakti on both sides;
with the infinite Veda in the middle, joined with a kundala...
(l. 3); Brahmā, seated upon a lotus.
Meditation on Durgā:
[She who has] the form of a thousand blue lotus petals,
with beautiful breasts and a lovely face, adorned with all ornaments.
[One should meditate on] the four-armed [Viṣṇu], joined with the thigh and the ashes of Mahiṣa’s head... (p. 38a, l. 1) (Side heading) (Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī) — The meditation on Viṣṇu:
Viṣṇu has four arms, wears a crown, and holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus;
he resembles a dark blue cloud and is seated upon Garuḍa. (l.
2) The meditation on Lakṣmī:
One should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī, who has four arms, bestowing the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons;
she who rests upon a lotus-stalk,
whose large eyes are like lotus flowers, and who is the beloved of Govinda.

...salutation to Vāsudeva. Salutation to Aniruddha. Salutation to Sāman. Salutation to Acyuta. Having worshipped [them], [the meditation on the upward *tāṇḍava*]—(side heading) Meditation on the Upward *Tāṇḍava*.
One-faced, three-eyed, with long arms and six limbs;
holding the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a *ḍamaru* drum, and a water-pot in his hands; with one hand placed on the tip of his foot, possessing a serpent-hand, and bearing fire.
Thus are the eight forms described, specifically with the feet pointing upwards;
the right foot is firmly planted while the left foot is raised...
[it is] served by Brahmā and others, as well as by Candra, Arka, and Nandikeśvara.
One should worship with the meditation-mantra the dance in the midst of the assembly, which is the embodiment of supreme bliss,
the immortal, the true, the stainless, the supreme secret, and the auspicious Śiva,
appearing in the form of Naṭeśa.

(Contemplation of the Goddess in the Vertical *Tāṇḍava* Pose) (p. 39a, l. 1) (Subheading) Contemplation of the Goddess: One should meditate upon Bhavānī, who has a dark complexion, two eyes, and two hands.
I worship her who holds a bracelet in her left hand and has a long, hanging trunk in her right;
(O Goddess, elephant-faced one), who possesses two arms and two eyes, and is adorned with a crown and a diadem.
With his left hand slightly contracted and his left face tremulous,
likewise on the right side he has a pure form, being victorious with a single arm alone;
he is one-faced, three-eyed, elephant-faced, red in color, and possesses four hands.

One should constantly meditate upon Vighneśvara, who is short and pot-bellied, with ears like winnowing baskets; he holds a *laḍḍuka* (sweetmeat) in his left hand and a goad made of a tusk in his right, with one foot tucked in sleep and the other leg raised and placed [upon the ground].
(The Bull, the Power of the Bull) (Side heading) The Sun, whose feet are the Vedas, whose horns are fire, whose eyes are the desired [objects],
whose face is the Lord of the Path (Vithīśin), and whose form is the ear of Aśvatī.
I bow to the King of Trees, whose body is adorned with jewels, gold, and garlands, who wears divine anklets and precious gems, and whose eyes are as white as crystal. (l.
3) [I bow to her] who has the luster of collyrium, three eyes of fire, and who bears camphor and sandalwood.
I pay homage to Añjanādevī, who possesses the splendor of musk, sandalwood, camphor, and saffron paste, and who is devoted to the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva). (Side heading:
Naṭeśvara)
Three-eyed, four-armed, and peaceful, adorned with a crown of matted locks;
wearing an earring of a crocodile on the right ear, and on the left,
a *dhurdhūra* ornament in his matted hair, topped by the crescent moon.
Joined with the *arkapuṣpa*, accompanied by the *bakapuṣpa*,
the *āragvadha*, and the *sṛj*, adorned above with a pillar;
on the right, the *jānhavī* and likewise the *vyāla* with its crest.
He places a skull-bowl (*karoti*) in his middle [left] hand, with a *kuṇḍa* and a gentle smile;
a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) in his right hand, and fire in his left hand.
Extending his left arm, he displays the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) together with a serpent’s hood.
The right foot is in the *svastika* position, while the left foot is bent;
she stands upon an *apasmāra* [demon] atop a *bhadrapīṭha* throne. (Devī: Her waist is encircled by a lion skin, and she wears a tiger skin as an upper garment.
Adorned with a garland of small bells, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
decorated with bracelets, necklaces, armlets, and anklets on his feet;
he stands in the midst of a circle of light, whether circular or likewise square.
Endowed with a white complexion and possessed of the thirty-two marks. (l.
4) The meditation on the Goddess: she has two arms, a beautiful face, and is endowed with two eyes. (l. 5)

Adorned with a crown and a jeweled casket, possessing dark blue locks of hair, with her hips broad and full... [she is] the Goddess, adorned with all ornaments, extending one hand while holding a lotus in her right hand.
Having meditated upon the goddess Dukkula... one should worship her with perfumes and other offerings.
Regarding the meditation on Caṇḍeśa:
he has one face and three eyes, and wears a jeweled crown and earrings.
One who is profound, a true brahmin, and possesses the topknot and the sacred thread.

Adorned with all ornaments, youthful and dark-complexioned; displaying the gesture of fearlessness with one hand on the thigh, while the other hand is joined in salutation; with the left foot [on the seat] and the right foot hanging down.
The seat with the right foot placed flat [and the left tucked behind] is the *sathānaka* posture.
The offering of the remains of the previous worship (*nirmālya*) should be made to Dhvani-Caṇḍeśvara. (Side heading:
Vighneśvara, Caṇḍa, Subrahmaṇya, Caṇḍa, Balināyaka)

O Caṇḍikeśa, you whose feet are Vakratuṇḍa, who are filled with the splendor of Bhoja, grant the fruit of service; salutations, salutations! O Subrahmaṇya, you whose feet are Vakratuṇḍa, who are filled with the splendor of Bhoja... [salutations, salutations!]
Grant the fruit of the propitiation of the planets; obeisance, obeisance to Sumitreśa! (l.3) The meditation on Śrī Balināyaka:
[He is] holding a black axe in his hand, which displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons. (l.4)
Kamalākara has four [eyes], and Candrabhānu has three eyes, like the sun and fire.
I bow to the lotus-feet of Śrī Bali, the leader of heroes, who wears a crown adorned with matted locks, stands in the *sthānaka* posture, and possesses the luster of coral.
(Side heading) (Meditation on Bhadrakālī) Meditation on Bhadrakālī: [She is] one-faced, three-eyed, with hair standing erect, and fully endowed [with ornaments].
Endowed with a dark complexion, adorned with four powerful arms,
the goddess has a serene countenance and is clothed in fine silk garments;
she holds a trident, a hand-drum, a skull-cup, and a noose.
She possesses great splendor, has wide-open eyes, and is adorned with serpent ornaments;
she is complete in all her limbs, yet her limbs are [pierced] by arrows. Her left foot rests upon the bed, while her right foot is hanging down.
Seated upon a divine lion-throne, adorned with divine garlands—having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess Bhadrakālī, may you be saluted. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Bhadrakālī.
(Bhadrakālī, Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī).
Dark-complexioned, wearing red garments, with a crest of flame like fire,
possessing eight arms and holding a trident, a vetāla, and a sword;
in her left hands she holds a *ḍamaru* drum and a skull-cup.
To her who has three eyes above [her other features], who holds a plow and a pestle, ...
(l. 3) ... to Cāmuṇḍī, adorned with all ornaments, the subduer of the world, to Bhadrakālī, salutations to you!
(l. 4) The meditation on Mahālakṣmī:

O Acyutā, who holds the hand of protection and the gesture of granting boons, bearing a pair of lotuses, adorned with red earrings, and possessing a complexion like the dawn; O Vajrasiddhalakṣmī, the mistress of the life of [your] Lord, salutations to you!

Sarasvatī, joined with the *dhyāna-daṣṭhī* [meditative gaze], with four... (p. 44a, l. 1) (Side heading: [Dhyāna of Durgā, the Goddess]) Holding a garland of lotuses in one hand, and also a white lotus and a parrot... (l. 2)
The goddess Durgā, whose speech shines like jasmine, the moon, a conch, and crystal, equal and ever-pleasing— may she dwell forever within [your] mouth. This is the meditation (*dhyāna*).
...the essence of fear, possessing great strength in the garment of her breasts, mounted upon a lion with even feet, [crushing] the buffalo... (p. 44b, l. 1) (Side heading) (Vimale):
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme definition of the Gaṇikā.
That [image], well-woven and endowed with auspicious marks,
will certainly bring prosperity to men at the outset and is worthy of divine worship.
It shall remain undamaged for three excellent years.
The commencement of learning should take place in the fifth year from conception;
marriage in the seventh year, while the twelfth year is considered the best.
Marriage performed in the eighth year is prescribed as middling.
From sixteen years onwards, [the age] is best, [and so on] down to the lowest. (l.

... protection... afterwards wrapped in a clean cloth. (p. 45a, l. 1)
Having honored the preceptor with garments, gold, and a ring,
one should invoke Śiva and worship the preceptor— who is joined by hand— with auspicious offerings.

Afterwards, with the permission of Mahādeva, one should perform the wearing of auspicious marks... (l. 4) ...one should cause the mudrās to be bestowed. Because of the authority over the five mudrās, it is thus arranged.
Having caused the garland to be given, [one performs] the wearing of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
Adorned with a bodice and beautified by [her] breasts,
one should cause her to offer a handful of flowers according to the measurements prescribed by Bharata.
Holding a water-pot upon her head, accompanied by all musical instruments, [she should perform].
"Having performed the circumambulation of the Ālaya, one should then join the *balipīṭha*";
thus it is stated in the *Vimala*.
The characteristics of the five mudrās:
the rudrākṣa [beads], the bodice on the breasts, the girdle at the waist, and [the ornaments] on the back and front;
it is similar to being endowed with a braided lock and a topknot.
Prostitutes [are] always [available] for people. Having performed the smearing with ashes, the wearing [of them], and so forth, and having recited the Śiva-mantra... (l.
6), and having meditated upon the daughters of Śaṅkara, one should have the Guru offer a water-pot to Śambhu. (p. 46a, l. 1)
In the middle petal of the trident-weapon, one should place Rudra in his undivided form;
in the left petals of Brahmā, Viṣṇu...
(l. 2); below that, a square, and likewise Pārvatī in the center.
On the right [side] are Sarasvatī and Mahālakṣmī;
on both sides are the moon and the sun; below are all the deities;
and likewise the world of the jar and the lunar deity.
I pay homage to the Buddha-avatāra, the deity who consists of the five elements and the four quarters, whose weapons are the trident and meditation,
who has two arms and one face, whose hand rests upon his thigh,
who sits upon a moving seat, and who wears the yogic belt.
Salutations to you, the one to whom all gods bow; you are the arrow that destroys Tripura, the exposition of the Dharmaśāstra, and the very nature of the Supreme Brahman.
For the sake of knowledge, absolute liberation, and mokṣa, one should meditate upon you, O Lord of the Boar, salutations to you!
(Side heading) (Subrahmaṇya, Meditation on the Chariot) The meditation on Bālasubrahmaṇya:
[He holds] a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a rosary (*akṣamālā*), as well as the gestures of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*) and bestowing boons (*varada*).
He should have a loincloth and even feet, adorned with all ornaments;
his body should be yellow and very serene, wearing a crown and jeweled earrings;
and he should have a sacred thread, a staff, and the Subrahmaṇya mantra.
The meditation on the chariot—(l.
4) ...and thereafter the sun, moon, and bow shall become composed of Brahman.
Thereafter, upon the seat... (l. 5)
...likewise Viṣṇuśailagaja;
and among all the deities, a quarter [of the total] follows that. *The asterism shall likewise be the ninth.* (l. 6)
And the serpent with its thread-binding;
the peak, partless... [with] *gaṃ* by means of chariot-threads;
likewise, for the devotees, the ṛṣis should be received with the five elements.
...(p.47a, l.1) (Side heading) (Meditation on Mahiṣāsuramardanī):
The meditation on the goddess Durgā—[she who holds] the Candrahāsa [sword]... [and] bears the conch, the discus, and the gesture of fearlessness. (l.2)
A bow, an arrow, a mace, a shield, and likewise a hand-drum; (l.3) a *va...* a *kunda*, an *akhaḍvāṅga*, and a plow-weapon;
a *droṇa*, a *kṣitīkā*, a piece of ground... (l.4) ...and a vessel for the mouth.
A silken cloth, a staff like a serpent, a wheel, a skull, a drum, a lute of Rudra, a skull-bowl, a noose, and a goad;
[the gestures of] fearlessness and the granting of boons— these are the thirty-two arms and weapons.
The goddess, possessing the luster of a ruby, like the rising sun...
(p. 47b, l. 1) (Side heading: Meditation on Naṭeśa) The goddess with two feet and two arms, worshipped within the circle of petals.
Having ten faces, two eyes, and endowed with full breasts,
wearing garments of red cloth and anointed with red perfumes;
likewise, she is the great flame that crushes the demon Mahiṣāsura.
The meditation on Naṭeśa:
four-armed and three-eyed, with a red complexion and a smiling face;
holding in his hands a skull-bowl and a *dhurdhurā* flower of the sun (*arka*).

He has a crest of matted hair with a young moon, possesses a beautiful complexion, and is engaged in playing with snakes; he stands upon an epileptic spirit. His right foot is bent, while his other foot is held level and extended.

In the right hand, however, there is a *pūrṇa* [vessel]...; in the other [right hand], an *ḍamaruka* drum is held. In the left hand, however, there is a *pūrva-kola* [vessel], and the other is a fire-vessel (*agni-pātraka*).
There should be a lotus leaf [in another hand], and in the right [hand], a conch-shell (*krakuṇḍala*).
He [should visualize] the one joined with Abhayā on the left...
(l. 3) ...and the one joined with Gaurī on the left, accompanied by Muravāri.
Thus, one should worship the form of Naṭeśa with the meditation-mantra. (l. 4)
(Side heading: *Dakṣiṇāmūrtti*, Meditation on Sadāśiva) The meditation on Dakṣiṇāmūrtti:
[He who has] fire, a pan, and matted hair, [and holds] the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*) and a rosary.
I bow to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who holds a lotus in his hand, whose garment is a tiger skin,
who is served by hosts of the best of gods and sages, who bears the moon upon his crest,
and who is adorned with various ornaments.
Seated upon a patch of ground near a banyan tree,
the bestower of knowledge to the people of the Kali age,
with a golden lute shimmering [in his hand], his brow and eyes slightly furrowed.
The meditation on Lord Sadāśiva Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who resides upon the peak of the best of mountains:
he has five faces resembling the moon and is endowed with ten hands.
In the right [hands], there should be a trident, a discus, a sword, and a thunderbolt;
in the left, a noose, a boon-granting gesture, a goad, a jewel, and fire.
His form is that of Sadāśiva seated upon a white lotus.
The goddess’s head is to the south and her foot to the north;
she is joined by arms holding water placed at the mouth and the end of the feet of a cow. (p. 49a, l.
1) (Side heading: Meditation on Bhuvaneśvarī, the Liṅga-Śakti, and Manonmanī)
The well-formed *liṅga* situated within the center of the *yoni*,
established as the very nature of Sadāśiva and Manonmanī;
[and she] holding a noose and a goad, bearing hands that grant boons and fearlessness.
[One should meditate on] her who wears yellow garments and is adorned with ornaments of gold and pearls... (l.
3) the single-syllabled one, who dwells upon a lotus held by the arts [of creation], the sovereign of the three worlds through her single syllable...
(l. 4) ...the meditation on the power of the *liṅga*.
With her left foot hanging down and her right foot resting upon a lotus seat,
two-armed and two-eyed,
with her hand placed upon a stool and holding a hundred-petaled lotus in her other hand.
I praise Miḍavāmamīḍā, whose limbs are as beautiful as a bud;
she is Manonmanī, dark-hued, with two eyes, two arms, and a triple-bent posture.
With her left foot placed forward and her right foot drawn back and bent,
she holds a blue lotus in her left hand and is adorned with bracelets; she is the Supreme Goddess who leans upon the hand of [her consort].
He holds the lotus of fearlessness and the boon-granting gesture, his limbs adorned with a rosary;
he has the color of a white lotus, a single face, and three eyes;
he wears garments of yellow silk and has the moon as his crest-jewel.
I shall worship the form of the Goddess, who supports and expands the vast earth.
(Verse 4) The meditation on Vīrabhadra:
In his right hands he holds a discus and a skull-topped staff, while his other hands shine with an axe; he possesses the lustrous splendor of a dark blue sapphire.

I worship Śrī Vīrabhadra, who holds a shield, a bow, a trident, and a serpent in his left hands; who is adorned with great ornaments, whose hair is aflame, who is saluted by the infinite multitude of spirits (*bhūta*), and who stands upon his right limb together with the three [deities] who are full and complete.

The Meditation on Vīrabhadra—(p. 50a, l. 1) (Sub-heading: The Meditation on Reṇukādevī)—[He is] three-eyed, with clouds in the sky... [and] joined palms as an offering to Dakṣa; he should be meditated upon as holding a sword in his left hand, a bracelet, and a bow. (l. 2)
...I worship the Hero who bears the moon, whose crown is a casket, who is in the form of a *liṅga*, standing in a posture with his left foot slightly raised... (l. 3)...
[I worship] Gāvyavīra.
The meditation on Goddess Reṇukā: she holds in her left hands a trident and a skull-cup,
while her other [right] hands bear a small drum and a lotus.
One should meditate on Śrī Reṇukā, who has three eyes, is radiant with the eight ornaments of a serpent,
possesses various shimmering ornaments like millions of suns at the end of an eon, and holds her other two husbands—
who are fast asleep and clinging to her right side.
(Side heading) (Meditation on Bhadrakālī):
She has one face and three eyes, with hair standing erect and blazing with fire;
she is endowed with a dark complexion and adorned with four staffs.
The goddess has a serene countenance and is clothed in fine linen;
she holds a trident, a hand-drum, a skull-cup, and a noose. She is radiant, possesses a third eye on her forehead, and is adorned with ornaments of serpents.
Ha... [she is] endowed with all her limbs clearly visible; her left foot is on the bed and her right foot is hanging down... (l. 4) ...sitting comfortably, adorned with divine garlands.
Having meditated thus upon the Great Goddess Bhadrakālī— (side heading) [the Vimāna and the Sthūpī]—
one should perform the meditation on the massive liṅga of the Vimāna:
two-footed, three-eyed, with a body adorned with ashes.
One should visualize [the deity] as having eight arms, equipped with a spear, a trident, a bow, ... a mace, and a lotus; ending in a *stūpa* and adorned with a crown;
with a broad body of red complexion.
(Side heading) (Meditation on Vāgīśvarī, Meditation on Vāgīśvara) Meditation on Vāgīśvarī:
Her body is dark-hued and she is in the full bloom of youth.
I meditate upon the mother of the supreme fire, whose hair is adorned with a garland of *soma* flowers, whose face is like the full moon, and who is full of nectar.
The meditation on Vāgīśvara:
[He is] three-eyed... (five-faced), white in color, four-armed, holding the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, the Lord of Vāgīśvarī.
The meditation on Bālāgni:
[He is] in the form of Bālāgni, with a body of red color, possessing three eyes...
[holding] a sacrificial ladle, a vessel of clarified butter, a fan, and a bell.
[He who holds] a spear and a rosary in his hands... (p. 52a, l. 1). (Side heading: *Sṛksṛvadhyāna*, [the meditation on] Vṛddhāgni).
Regarding the *Sṛksṛvadhyāna*:
the *sṛksṛva* is the spear and Śambhu, with two openings at its mouth. (l. 2).

Śuddhavidyā is the resonance (nāda). Resonance is the state consisting of nectar, the root of food and the eater, conjoined with that which is purified by mantra, having the stalk beginning with the moon, [attaining] deep sleep through the channels (gaṇḍī) and the upward-moving breaths, produced from the staff, beginningless.
The meditation on Vṛddhāgni:
[He is] tawny-limbed, three-eyed, and wears a crown of matted hair... (l.

[The one on] the bull-throne... (p.53b, l.1) (Side heading) (The bull of the *ālaya*, the god of Dharma)...
wearing a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
The god is clothed in a tiger skin, ever-maintaining the sacrificial fire, and possessing the form of an elder. (l.2)
A white-colored bull with one face, four legs, and a belly shaped like a donkey’s, possessing sharp majesty and strength;

For one who has sons equal... (l. 2) and likewise with the single-footed hand.

(Side heading) (Gaṇeśa together with his mouse vehicle) Gaṇeśa, who has a human form, elephant ears, and an elephant face;
who has a large belly, a massive body, a single tusk, and three eyes. (l. 2)
In his right hand he holds a goad-staff, and on his left side a *tulāḍḍuka* fruit;
his palm is joined with the tip of an elephant’s trunk.
He is endowed with a white complexion and is mounted upon a mouse as his vehicle.
One should worship this form of Gaṇeśa with [offerings] beginning from the left foot.
(Side heading: Subrahmaṇya accompanied by his peacock vehicle) He is endowed with four arms, two eyes, and two feet.
Endowed with a dark complexion, [he should visualize] the peacock’s... (l. 2).
One should fashion a crown of various jewel-forms, a turban, and an upper garment; one should also provide ear-ornaments and a cluster of flowers for the hair-tuft. (l. 3)
Endowed with a vajra and a spear, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
clothed in various garments and adorned with all ornaments;
on the left side is the Yoginī, and on the right side is the Bhoginī.
Saffron is red in color, and it is said to be the form of the Goddess.
The blue lotus is the syllable *vaṃ*, having a peaceful appearance; [he who possesses it] is the Lord of the Gods, whose navel is a lotus and who reclines upon the serpent.

I bow to Viṣṇu, the support of the universe, resembling the sky, cloud-colored, with auspicious limbs; the beloved of Lakṣmī, lotus-eyed, attainable through meditation by yogis, the remover of worldly existence, and the sole lord of all the worlds.
He whose feet are the earth, whose navel is the ocean, whose breath is the wind, whose eyes are the moon and sun, whose ears are the quarters,
whose speech is the Vedas, whose head is heaven, and whose garment is the deep abyss; he within whom the entire universe resides—
along with gods, men, birds, serpents, gandharvas, and daityas— and whose limbs are the world.
"O delightful one... I bow to [the one] of all the worlds. (p. 55a, l.
1) Śukra, seated upon the lion-throne, returned once more to heaven as he had attained it... (l.
2) Then, while [he was] standing, [he saw] the goddess with her hands joined in the *naṣṭābja* gesture. (l. 3)
I bow to the mother of all worlds, born from the ocean;
to Śrī, whose eyes are like blossoming lotuses, who resides upon the chest of Viṣṇu; to her whose abode is the lotus, whose hands hold lotuses, and whose glances are like lotus petals.
I bow to the goddess Padmāmukhī, the beloved of Padmanābha. You are Siddhi, you are Amṛtā, you are Svāhā. (p. 55b, l.

To those whose path leads to our lotus-like nectar, I shall summon them all; here is this water with sesame seeds. From Brahmā down to those born in my paternal lineage, and from my mother’s side, [those] of auspicious and noble descent.
In these two lineages, my slaves, as well as servants and those who serve me without wages, the friends of my friend, animals, trees,
those touched by me, the wicked, and those who have benefited the wheel— may I be unattached to them in another birth.
I offer this *svadhā* rice-ball (*piṇḍa*).
To those deceased in the paternal lineage and likewise in the maternal lineage; to teachers, fathers-in-law, brothers-in-law, kinsmen, and other relatives who have died;
to those in my family for whom the *piṇḍa* offerings have been interrupted, and who are destitute of sons and wives.

And those known in my lineage whose rites were neglected, whose funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) were withheld from them because they were deprived of sons and wives; those who were struck by the omission of rites, those remembered as born of mud, the deformed, and those with immature fetuses—(l.
4) for all those known in my lineage, their funeral cakes have been offered, which are inexhaustible... (l. 5)
In the terrible Aśīpatra forest and in the Raurava hell of trembling heat, for the sake of their deliverance, I shall inflict punishment upon them. By the merit bestowed by this family,
may the honey-cake offered to these [beings]— who have been given [libations] by the lineage— stand before them as nectar.
May the sages, ancestors, and humans, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass,
and all the ancestors— maternal grandfathers, paternal grandfathers, and the rest— be satisfied by this water mixed with sesame seeds.
Whatever exists within the limits of the universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, including all that is mobile and immobile— may it be satisfied.
May you attain satisfaction with this water offered by me.
[Prayer:
O my ancestors, who exist in the form of certain *preta*s, may you attain satisfaction through these *tilodaka* offerings presented by Kuśa.

One who has white leprosy, one with skin disease, as well as one who is ill, one who is deceitful, one who speaks harshly, a friend of the wicked, a slanderer of the Sun, a thief, a seller of the Vedas, one who delights in [sensual] pleasure, one who abandons his mother, father, or guru, one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*, and the son of a *śūdra* woman— Kusha,
having asked for water with sesame seeds, brings satisfaction to them.

One should perform the washing at the base of the feet for the father, at the middle of the feet for the grandfather, and at the tips of the feet for the great-grandfather; thus perform the washing of the feet. This cleansing of the feet is without oil massage, without sesame seeds, and without mantras.
In the *śrāddha* rite, if the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is lacking, the ancestors depart in despair.
One should perform [the rite] in the proper sequence; whether seated or standing, endowed with splendor and complete union.
The characteristic [of the deity] has been declared; one should worship in the western direction.
May it be auspicious!
